title: The Wheat and the Weeds
hook: Does a farming joke about weeds really describe people burning forever?
tldr: Jeremy Myers (Redeeming God) reads this parable as Jesus' answer to his disciples' dilemma: follow Jesus or the Pharisees? Don't uproot anything yourselves; wait for the harvest at the end of this age, when God's angels burn up the bad teaching. He places that harvest at Jerusalem's fall in AD 70. Endless torture is nowhere in view.
big_idea: Let God sort good teaching from bad; the fire is not hell.

points.title: God's reign on earth, not heaven
points.text: Myers: nobody in Jesus' day thought the kingdom of God meant heaven. It was God's rule on earth replacing Rome. All seven parables of Matthew 13 are about that kingdom, not the afterlife.

points.title: A joke about a silly enemy
points.text: Fields grow weeds without help, so an enemy sowing weeds would make hearers snicker. The weed is likely darnel, a mimic of wheat that sickens or kills if eaten in quantity.

points.title: The unexplained servants are the key
points.text: Jesus decodes sower, field, seed, weeds, enemy, harvest and reapers, but not the servants. Myers: they are his disciples, the workers in the field, told not to do the uprooting themselves.

points.title: Sons of… means character
points.text: Sons of light, sons of the Pharisees, sons of disobedience: the idiom describes character, not birth. Sons of the kingdom and sons of wickedness are two kinds of people shaped by two kinds of teaching.

points.title: The harvest came in AD 70
points.text: A harvest thousands of years away would not help the disciples choose. Myers ties the end of this age to Jerusalem and the temple burning in AD 70, when the Pharisees' way died and Christianity survived.

points.title: Daniel's furnace burned only bonds
points.text: The furnace image comes from Daniel 3:19-25, where only the young men's bonds burned while one like a son of God walked with them. The Son of Man and the shining righteous also come from Daniel.

points.title: Weeping is for the family
points.text: All six uses of weeping and gnashing of teeth in Matthew concern people who belonged to God in some way. Myers reads it as regret, shame and fury, not torment in hell.

sections.summary: Myers starts with the context of Matthew 13. Its parables have puzzled interpreters ever since, and even the disciples asked for explanations (Matthew 13:10, 36). Jesus said one reason he used parables was so that people would not understand (Matthew 13:15-16), so that those who wanted to learn would come to him. If a parable confuses you, you are on the right track; let it lead you to Jesus.

Myers gives three keys. First, use whatever symbolism Jesus himself explains. Second, learn the historical, cultural and theological context: what matters is what the original audience heard, so enter their times, culture, way of reading the Hebrew Bible and their concerns, not ours. Third, Jesus had a sense of humour: half-jokes, wordplay and surprising twists meant to amuse and teach.

sections.h: The kingdom of God versus Rome
sections.summary: Most of Jesus' parables are about the kingdom of God. Today people hear heaven, but nobody in Jesus' day did. They suffered daily under the kingdom of Rome and longed for the Messiah to overthrow it. So the kingdom of God is God's rule and reign on earth, here and now, replacing the kingdoms of men.

sections.h: Jewish hearers and a subversive message
sections.summary: His hearers were nearly all Jews steeped in the Hebrew Scriptures, so Old Testament concepts, imagery and themes are needed to understand the parables. And the parables were politically and religiously subversive, not mainly against Rome as people hoped, but against the politics and religion of Judaism. That is one reason Jesus veiled them: the ruling class would have crucified him sooner.

sections.h: Seven kingdom parables, none about the afterlife
sections.summary: Matthew 13 holds seven parables about the kingdom of heaven. Not one is about going to heaven when you die or proving you are a real Christian; all describe the nature, character, birth and growth of God's kingdom on earth. The Four Soils shows how people respond to kingdom teaching, and anyone can be any soil. Its sower scatters valuable seed carelessly: God has never cared much for efficiency.

The kingdom is like a man sowing good seed in his field; heaven coming down to earth as Jesus and his disciples spread God's reign. Read with the Four Soils, the seed is the word of God. But here two kinds of seed are sown, the seeds of the kingdom and the seeds of the devil: two contrasting kingdoms producing two contrasting kinds of people, hard to tell apart at first.

Anyone with a field or even a flower garden knows weeds pop up without an enemy's help. So when Jesus described an enemy sneaking in to sow weeds, his audience would likely have snickered. No enemy would work so hard to ruin a crop; there were easier ways. The enemy's effort shows his own foolishness and gives the whole story a humorous backdrop.

The bad seed is most likely darnel, which looks just like wheat until harvest. Pulling it early would uproot wheat too, so the owner says to let both grow (Matthew 13:27-30). The servants only notice once the grain heads form. At harvest wheat turns golden and its heavy heads droop, while darnel stays greener longer and keeps standing upright.

Reapers gather the tares first and burn them, then harvest the wheat. Myers explains why: darnel can be deadly to livestock and people in large quantities, and smaller amounts baked into bread or brewed into beer cause dizziness. There are historical records of people cultivating it for that effect, like an ancient form of cannabis, but too much brings great sickness and even death.

Jesus explains this one. The sower is the Son of Man, his favourite title for himself. The field is the world. The good seed is the sons of the kingdom; the tares are their opposite, the sons of the wicked one (perhaps better, sons of wickedness). The enemy is the devil, the harvest the end of the age, the reapers the angels (Matthew 13:37-39).

One set of characters goes unexplained: the servants. Myers calls this missing identification the key to the parable. They are not the reapers, since the owner names the reapers as a separate group (Matthew 13:30). They work and tend the field, which is the world, so they are Jesus' followers, his disciples. That means the seed, the sons of the kingdom, must be someone else.

Son can be a metaphor. Tied to an idea rather than a family, it describes someone's character. Sons of this world versus sons of light (Luke 16:8; John 12:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). A disciple of the Pharisees is a son of the Pharisees (Matthew 12:27; Acts 23:6). Also sons of the resurrection (Luke 20:36), of disobedience (Ephesians 2:2), of the devil (Acts 13:10).

Just before these parables, the religious leaders said Jesus worked by Beelzebub (Matthew 12:24). His reply uses imagery that returns in Matthew 13: kingdoms, sons of the Pharisees, gathering and scattering, this age and the age to come, and fruitful or fruitless trees (Matthew 12:25-37). He said it was they who blasphemed and spoke evil from their hearts. All of Matthew 13 must be read in light of this confrontation.

How could the onlookers tell who was right? The disciples had grown up loving and heeding the Pharisees, and now loved and heeded Jesus. Each side said the other's teaching was from the devil. It is like two respected Bible teachers who disagree. The parable is Jesus' answer: two kinds of seed have produced two kinds of sons of two kingdoms. Wait for the harvest.

sections.h: This age and the age to come
sections.summary: Waiting until the end of this age would not help if it lay thousands of years away. Myers proposes this age was the one Jesus and the disciples lived in, and the age to come the one that followed (Matthew 12:32). Jesus' death and resurrection and the church's birth began a new age, with birth pains as the old age died, as Matthew 24-25 describes.

Here is the parable's subversive edge. The disciples must choose between the way of Jesus and the way of the Pharisees, yet Jesus says they need not sort it out. Trying would be dangerous, for they cannot perfectly tell good teaching from bad. They should wait and let the reaping angels separate them. Myers says this happened in AD 70, when Jerusalem and the temple burned.

This does not mean the Pharisees and their followers will burn forever; everlasting torture is not in view. The furnace of fire comes from Daniel 3:19-25, where Daniel's friends are thrown in but only their bonds burn, and one like a son of God walks with them in the flames. The Son of Man comes from Daniel 7:13-14, and the righteous shining like the sun from Daniel 12:3.

Many Christians probably died in the flames when Rome destroyed Jerusalem. But Christianity survived, because it did not depend on a city, a temple or a priesthood. The Pharisaic religion did, and Myers says it died out when Jerusalem fell. Since Genesis 3, humans have judged good and evil poorly, so God invites us to leave such judgment to him.

sections.h: Six uses of weeping and gnashing
sections.summary: The phrase occurs six times in Matthew (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30), once in Luke (13:28), nowhere else. Every Matthew use concerns people who are part of the family: sons of the kingdom; those gathered out of the kingdom, so once in it; fish in the same net; a man at the wedding banquet; servants who served their master poorly.

So the phrase is about people who belonged to God in some way and should have known his expectations: believers facing a hard time at the judgment seat of Christ or God's discipline now, or Jews who should have recognised their Messiah. It is a graphic Middle Eastern way of expressing profound regret, shame, maybe fury. Edward Fudge: weeping speaks of extreme loss more than pain; gnashing may be anger at someone else.

Matthew 13:42 and 13:50 do not picture God casting people into everlasting flames to scream forever. Jesus means that when judgment comes after the end of the age, which Myers says ended at Jesus' resurrection, good and bad teaching will be made plain: one survives, one burns up. That judgment fell in AD 70, a day of flames and of much weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Josephus (Wars of the Jews 6.5.3) reports that before Rome burned the city, chariots and armed troops were seen running among the clouds, and at Pentecost priests felt a quaking and heard a multitude saying, Let us remove hence. He admits it sounds like a fable but says many saw it. Myers asks: could these be the angels of Matthew 13:39-41, separating the harvest?

The parable is not about God sending sinners to burn for all eternity. It is a prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish religion as then practised, and a lesson that Jesus' disciples should not try to judge between his teaching and their own Jewish traditions. God and the angels would make the separation themselves, and did in AD 70.

sections.h: Other evidence and other non-ECT readings
sections.summary: Beyond Myers: Roman law dealt with sowing weeds in another's field (Digest 9.2.27.14), so the scenario was not impossible. Sunteleia tou aionos means completion of an age; the disciples use it about the temple (Matthew 24:3), and Hebrews 9:26 sets it in the first century. Conditionalists stress katakaio, burn up: R.T. France saw destruction, not endless torment. Restorationists cite Malachi's refining fire. Andrew Perriman sees AD 70 as foretaste of final judgment.

Traditional commentators such as GotQuestions and BibleRef read the furnace as hell at the final judgment, with weeping and gnashing showing conscious, unending anguish of the unrepentant. Critics reply that the parable never says the fire lasts forever or that the weeds survive it, and Jesus' explanation never adds the word eternal.

parable.audience: The crowds by the lake; then the disciples in the house, who asked Jesus to explain it.
parable.setting: Right after the Pharisees said Jesus worked by Beelzebub (Matthew 12:24-37). Seven kingdom parables told to Jews longing for God to replace Rome, while the disciples were torn between Jesus and the Pharisees.

visuals.title: Reading the furnace closely
visuals.text: As the weeds are pulled up and burned in the fire, so it will be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send out his angels, and they will weed out of his kingdom everything that causes sin and all who do evil. They will throw them into the blazing furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

mythfact.myth: The parable teaches that the wheat go to heaven and the weeds to hell.
mythfact.fact: Myers: all seven Matthew 13 parables describe God's kingdom growing on earth. The command is to the servants: don't uproot; let God sort good teaching from bad.

mythfact.myth: Sons of the evil one means people born to be damned.
mythfact.fact: Sons of… is an idiom for character: sons of light, sons of the Pharisees, sons of disobedience. It describes what shapes a person, not a fixed destiny.

mythfact.myth: The furnace of fire is a picture of hell.
mythfact.fact: It comes from Daniel 3, where the faithful walked in the furnace and only their bonds burned. Myers ties the parable's fire to Jerusalem burning in AD 70.

mythfact.myth: Weeping and gnashing of teeth describes outsiders tormented in hell.
mythfact.fact: All six uses in Matthew concern insiders: sons of the kingdom, a wedding guest, servants. It expresses regret, shame or fury.

objections.claim: Jesus himself says the weeds are people, the sons of the evil one, so this is about the eternal fate of the wicked.
objections.strongest: Jesus' own interpretation leaves no room for allegorizing: the weeds are persons, the furnace awaits them at the end, and the righteous shine. A plain reading is a final judgment with two eternal destinies.
objections.response: Sons of… is a character idiom (sons of light, sons of the Pharisees, sons of disobedience), so the weeds are people shaped by a rival teaching, not a damned class. Myers reads the fire as burning up that teaching when Jerusalem fell, with no one sent to hell. Even granting final judgment of persons, weeds in fire are burned up (katakaio), the furnace is Daniel's, where only bonds burned, and the parable never says eternal. Conditionalists read destruction; Perriman sees AD 70 as a foretaste.

objections.claim: The end of the age is the end of history, the final judgment, not a first-century event.
objections.strongest: Matthew 28:20 promises Jesus' presence until the end of the age, which seems to stretch beyond AD 70. The angels gather from the whole kingdom, and the righteous shining fits the resurrection of Daniel 12, not a war.
objections.response: Myers answers from the parable's purpose: a harvest thousands of years away would not help disciples choosing between Jesus and the Pharisees. Matthew 12:32 already contrasts this age with the age to come, and the disciples tie the phrase to the temple's fall (Matthew 24:3); Hebrews 9:26 sets the completion of the ages in the first century. Readers who keep a future judgment, like Perriman, still see AD 70 as its preview. Either way, the age's end decides who belongs, not how long anyone burns.

objections.claim: Weeping and gnashing of teeth proves the people in the furnace are conscious and suffering, so this is hell.
objections.strongest: You cannot weep if you no longer exist. Lexical studies show gnashing expresses anguish and rage, and BibleRef reads the phrase as Jesus' language for the eternal fate of the unrepentant.
objections.response: Myers notes all six Matthew uses describe insiders: sons of the kingdom, those gathered out of the kingdom, a wedding guest, unfaithful servants. That fits regret at loss, not outsiders in torment; Fudge calls it extreme loss more than actual pain, and gnashing can be fury at someone else, which Stephen Cook's study also stresses. Luke 13:28 sets the weeping at the moment of exclusion. Nothing in seven uses says it never ends.

objections.claim: The Pharisees did not vanish in AD 70; their movement became rabbinic Judaism, so the AD 70 reading fails.
objections.strongest: Historians note Pharisaic schools continued after the temple fell and shaped rabbinic Judaism. If the weeds were the Pharisees' way and the fire destroyed it, the history does not match Myers' claim that it died out.
objections.response: This is a fair challenge to Myers' wording. His point is that a religion dependent on city, temple and priesthood could not go on in that form once Jerusalem burned, while Jesus' way needed none of them. Judaism did survive, but reshaped around Torah study and prayer without sacrifice. Readers who find the AD 70 link too narrow still have other non-ECT options: the weeds are consumed, or refined. The objection weakens one interpretation, not the case against eternal torment.
